overview: This file documents U.S. consular reporting from Dairen on alien employment and immigration controls in the Japanese-administered Kwantung Leased Territory. A 1932 despatch reports that no formal restrictions limited alien employment and that Chinese workers could enter subject to police examination. A 1934 despatch gives a more qualified picture: arriving foreign workers had to possess adequate means, avoid manual “coolie” labor and political or communist activity, and normally provide evidence of employment with a reputable concern; Russians received especially close scrutiny. Cross-reference sheets connect both despatches to other State Department decimal files, while an enclosed translation of Kwantung Government Ordinance No. 15 supplies part of the legal framework governing admission to the leased territory and the South Manchuria Railway Zone.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for Despatch No. 6 on alien employment restrictions
subfiles.about: The sheet refers researchers to file 800.504/36 for Despatch No. 6 concerning alien employment restrictions in the Kwantung Leased Territory.
subfiles.summary: The filing note records that there were no restrictions on the employment of aliens in the Kwantung Leased Territory. It states that a copy of the despatch is attached and directs the reader to another decimal file for the official despatch.

subfiles.title: Despatch on alien employment restrictions in the Kwantung Leased Territory
subfiles.about: Vincent reports on whether the Kwantung Leased Territory restricted the employment of foreign nationals.
subfiles.summary: Responding to a State Department instruction prompted by a letter from the Secretary of Labor, Vincent reports that no restrictions were placed on alien employment. He observes that Dairen was unlikely to attract American or European job seekers. Chinese entrants could freely seek employment, subject only to police examination of the nature of their business.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for Despatch No. 107 on the labor situation
subfiles.about: The sheet identifies Despatch No. 107 concerning the temporary admission and residence of aliens seeking employment in the Kwantung Territory.
subfiles.summary: The filing note directs readers to file 894c.55/7 for Despatch No. 107. It describes the despatch as a report based on information from the Kwantung Government Marine Police and notes the enclosure of a translation of Ordinance No. 15 of March 20, 1918.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 107 on special immigration and foreign workers
subfiles.about: Vincent reports the conditions under which performers and other foreign workers could enter and reside in the Kwantung Leased Territory.
subfiles.summary: An interpreter for the Kwantung Government Marine Police told the consulate that performers and other foreign workers were not governed by separate entry rules. Aliens had to possess sufficient means, refrain from seeking manual “coolie” labor, and avoid political activity or communist agitation; Russians were confidentially said to receive closer examination than other nationalities. Applicants with concrete evidence of employment by a reputable concern generally encountered little difficulty, although the requested statistics were unavailable. Vincent enclosed a translation of the 1918 ordinance regulating alien admission.

subfiles.title: Translation of Kwantung Government Ordinance No. 15
subfiles.about: The enclosure sets out regulations governing foreign entry into the Kwantung Leased Territory and the South Manchuria Railway Zone.
subfiles.summary: The OCR for the first page of the enclosure is illegible and records only the presence of handwritten material. The surviving second page contains Articles 5–8, permitting officials to exclude or expel persons who obtained entry through false statements. It exempts diplomats, consular officers, official missions, their families, and crews of vessels belonging to the high contracting powers, and includes rules on commencement and transitional passport exceptions.

interest: The file is valuable for the contrast between the consulate’s categorical 1932 assertion that alien employment was unrestricted and its more detailed 1934 account of practical screening and exclusion. Especially revealing are the confidential admission that Russians received heightened scrutiny and the linking of labor control to poverty, racialized occupational categories, and fear of communist agitation. The cross-reference sheets also expose the State Department’s filing practices, while the ordinance enclosure connects consular observations to the formal legal machinery of Japanese colonial administration; however, the OCR loss on page 6 leaves part of that legal text inaccessible.
